title: The Priority Queue Behind the Heap
quickIdea: A binary heap is the standard implementation of a priority queue: the extreme is O(1) away, insert and delete-extreme are O(log n), but merging two heaps costs Theta(n) and deleting a key you can only name costs Theta(n) to find it first.
remember: The abstract data type: insert(x), minimum or maximum, delete-min or delete-max, plus decrease-key, increase-key, delete(x) and merge.

Costs on a binary heap of n keys: find-extreme O(1); insert O(log n) worst case and O(1) average; delete-extreme O(log n); decrease-key O(log n) once the position is known; delete(x) O(log n) after an O(n) search; merge Theta(n); build Theta(n).

A key change is two different repairs by direction: toward the root (an increase in a max-heap, a decrease in a min-heap) needs sift-up, and away from the root needs sift-down. One name, two procedures.

decrease-key needs a handle to the position. A plain array heap has no map from key to slot, which is why the O(log n) figure is conditional and why Dijkstra's implementation stores the index of each vertex.
Against the alternatives: an unsorted list gives insert Theta(1) but delete-min Theta(n); a sorted list gives the reverse; the heap balances both at Theta(log n), which is why it is the default.

Conversions: any array becomes a heap in Theta(n), so a BST becomes a max-heap in Theta(n) by walking it and building. A heap does not become a BST in Theta(n), because that would sort in linear time.

example.prompt: A heap holds 1000 keys. Give the worst-case cost of find-max, insert, delete-max and merging it with another heap of 500 keys.
example.work: The height is floor(log2 1000) = 9. find-max reads A[1], one step. insert appends and climbs at most 9 levels, so at most 9 swaps. delete-max moves the last key up and sinks at most 9 levels. Merging is not supported cheaply: the two arrays are concatenated, giving 1500 cells, and one build-heap runs over them, which is Theta(1500).
example.answer: find-max O(1); insert O(log n); delete-max O(log n); merge Theta(n), here about 1500 steps against 500 * log(1500) for 500 separate insertions.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2019 Q.40 is the operations-and-conversion question: it prices a heap build at Theta(n) and refuses the reverse conversion for exactly the reason given here. The two costs most often mis-stated are delete of a named key and merge.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2019 Q.40, statement IV. 'A binary search tree can be constructed from a max-heap in Theta(n) time.' Is it true?
variations.why: Any array becomes a heap in Theta(n), so if a heap became a BST in Theta(n) as well, an inorder walk (Theta(n)) would sort n keys in Theta(n) with comparisons, contradicting the Omega(n log n) lower bound. Extracting the keys in sorted order costs Theta(n log n), and inserting them one by one into a BST costs Theta(n log n) on average and Theta(n^2) in the worst case.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: You hold two binary heaps of 500 keys each and must produce one heap. What is the cheapest correct cost?
variations.answer: Theta(n) for n = 1000: append the two arrays and run one build-heap.
variations.why: A binary heap has no cheap merge: inserting the 500 keys of one heap into the other costs 500 * O(log 1000). Concatenating the arrays gives 1000 cells that are not a heap, but build-heap makes them one in Theta(1000). Merging is Theta(n), which is why meldable heaps exist for the applications that need it.

trap.what: Quoting the deletion of an arbitrary key as O(log n) in a plain array heap.
trap.why: The sink after the removal is O(log n), but only once the position is known. Nothing in the array maps a key to its index, so locating the key is a scan of the whole array, and the operation as a whole is Theta(n).
trap.counterexample: In a 1000-key heap you are told to delete the key 37. The search for 37 is Theta(n) in the worst case, and only then does the O(log n) repair begin, so the total is Theta(n). The O(log n) figure belongs to the case where the position was handed to you, as Dijkstra's algorithm arranges.

check.question: Which priority-queue operation is Theta(n) on a binary heap even when the element's position is known in advance?
check.explanation: Merging two binary heaps means concatenating the arrays and rebuilding, which is Theta(n) because build-heap is Theta(n). delete-min is O(log n) when the position is known, insert is O(log n), and find-min is O(1). Melding in O(log n) needs a different structure, such as a binomial or Fibonacci heap, and those are outside the GATE CSE syllabus line.
